title: The great collections, closed
hook: the Connected and the Numbered Sayings

segments.voice: Yesterday: three listeners and three pots, and your line, keep the pot upright. Did something stay in? Today we close a whole part of the path, and see what the pot holds. Day six hundred eighty.

Forty-five days ago this part of the path opened with two great libraries. The Samyutta Nikaya, the Connected Sayings. The Anguttara Nikaya, the Numbered Sayings. Together they hold thousands of short discourses, many no longer than a page. Long discourses are like novels. These are more like a box of letters: a question asked at a roadside, an image tossed off before a meal, a list counted on the fingers. Since then you've crossed the flood, seen Mara named, taken apart a chariot, felt the second arrow, watched foam on the river, and pulled your ears. Today we close both books. Today: the great collections.
screen: `TWO GREAT LIBRARIES.` → `A BOX OF SHORT LETTERS.` → `FORTY-FIVE DAYS.`

segments.voice: Start with how they're built, because that's the point of today's line. The Connected Sayings gathers its suttas by kind. Fifty-six groups, each on one theme or one speaker: a chapter of verses with gods, a chapter on Mara, a chapter on the five aggregates, one on the sense bases, one on mindfulness. Read it and you see a subject turned over a hundred ways. That's where you met the chariot of parts, the burden, the dog on its leash, all is burning, the eye as an ocean, the nuns and the inspiring sign, and the old Buddha in the sun. The Numbered Sayings gathers its suttas by number. The Book of Ones, the Book of Twos, all the way up to Elevens. Three intoxications. Four kinds of people, and the firebrand. Five remembrances. Five ways to remove a grudge. Six ways to be dear. Seven marks of a friend. Eight winds. Ten perceptions at a sick bed. Eleven blessings of metta. Why sort teaching by number? Scholars point out that these texts were passed on by memory, chanted by monks for centuries before they were written down. A list of five is easier to carry than a paragraph. Each way of sorting shows you something. By kind, you go deep into one subject. By number, you get a toolkit, a handful of things to count on your fingers on an ordinary Tuesday. And across both, the same teacher keeps speaking to monks and nuns, kings and farmers, couples and the sick, in the plainest images he could find.
screen: `BY KIND: FIFTY-SIX GROUPS.` · `BY NUMBER: ONES TO ELEVENS.` · `MADE TO BE REMEMBERED.` · then, large: `BY KIND AND BY NUMBER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pick one line from each. Sit, and settle. Let the Connected Sayings pass by: the flood, the tangle, one arrow, foam on the river, the burden, all is burning, inspired then calm, even his. Which one stays? Hold it. Now let the Numbered Sayings pass: remember me as awake, for self and others, heir to my deeds, eight winds, toward less, sleep in peace, a friend gives the hard thing. Which one stays? Hold both lines together for a few breaths. The bell holds the time.
The great collections. The Samyutta Nikaya, sorted by theme, and the Anguttara Nikaya, sorted by number: thousands of short discourses, made to be remembered. Today's word.
Your line: by kind and by number. Today, carry your two chosen lines, one from each book, and say each once before bed. Tomorrow, a new part: the festival year. Day six hundred eighty.

screen: `DAY 680 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE MOON KEEPS THE CALENDAR.`

howItsDone: Monastics in the Theravada tradition still memorize and chant suttas from the Connected and Numbered Sayings, and many lay study groups read them one short discourse at a time.

fork.setup: you need to pass on thousands of teachings, by memory alone, for centuries. how might you sort them?
options: by theme, and by number of items.
by the date each was given.
fork.reveal: the Connected Sayings sort by theme, the Numbered Sayings by number. both are ways to make a huge body of teaching memorable.

original.note: Pali samyutta: connected, joined together; the Samyutta Nikaya is the 'connected' collection.

trapdoor: what you thought: Buddhist scripture is one long book.
what it means: the Pali discourses come in several collections, two sorted by kind and by number.
what a scholar hears: anguttara means 'one more,' 'going up by one': the collection climbs from ones to elevens.
